note: Compares regulatory approaches across the United States, EU, Asia, Africa and the Americas, and proposes adaptive rules that can move at the pace of the technology rather than the pace of legislation.
title: Managing the race to the moon: Global policy and governance in Artificial Intelligence regulation
explain_beginner: As countries race to build more powerful AI, this paper asks how governments around the world are trying to write rules for it, and whether those rules can keep up with how fast the technology changes. The author compares several very different approaches, the European Union's system that sorts AI uses into risk categories and regulates the riskiest ones most heavily, the United States' looser, innovation-focused approach built around voluntary guidance and an executive order, China's specific laws targeting things like deepfakes and recommendation algorithms, and emerging strategies in Japan, Singapore, India, Canada, and Latin America. The paper finds that these approaches are pulling in different directions, creating a patchwork of rules rather than one shared standard, and that lawmaking is generally too slow to match how quickly AI capabilities are advancing. The author calls for more flexible, 'dynamic' laws that bring government and industry together on an ongoing basis, and notes that AI's effects on jobs, democracy, and the reliability of information are still not well understood.
explain_business: Any organization deploying AI across more than one country is dealing with a genuinely fragmented compliance landscape, and this paper's comparison makes the scale of that fragmentation concrete, an AI system built to satisfy the EU's risk-tiered rules is not automatically compliant with the United States' more decentralized approach or China's specific, application-by-application laws. Because the paper argues that regulation is generally struggling to keep pace with AI development, and calls for more adaptive, 'dynamic' rulemaking that keeps evolving with industry input, businesses should expect the compliance target to keep moving rather than settling into one final, stable rulebook anytime soon. The practical implication for legal, policy, and product teams is to build flexible, modular compliance processes region by region, and to engage directly in policy conversations rather than assuming a single global AI governance standard will emerge quickly. This paper does not change what AI can do technically, it changes how much legal and reputational risk surrounds deploying it across different markets.
explain_practitioner: The paper takes a comparative policy analysis approach, combining literature review with examination of primary policy documents, the EU AI Act, the United States executive order on AI, China's issue-specific laws on deepfakes, recommendation algorithms, and facial recognition, and national strategies from Japan, Singapore, India, Canada, and Latin American countries, illustrated with cases such as AI-generated media and social credit systems. There is no quantitative dataset or benchmark, the contribution is a structured comparison rather than an empirical test. The central finding is that regulatory philosophy diverges sharply by region, the EU's tiered risk classification, the United States' decentralized, innovation-first stance, and China's vertical, application-specific laws, producing global fragmentation that complicates compliance for organizations operating across borders. The paper proposes 'dynamic laws' that combine formal government authority with continuous industry input as a way to keep pace with AI development. The authors name a specific limitation, a gap in the literature on AI governance's socioeconomic dimensions, and note that details on real-world enforcement and compliance are thin for some countries, including Ukraine and Russia.
